Mr. Speaker, I also am pleased to rise on Bill C-97. My colleagues have expanded in some detail about the financial aspects of this bill. We have said, of course, that our party is opposed to Bill C-97 for a number of reasons. First of all, we oppose this bill in principle because it is an autocratic, unilateral action on the part of the federal government. It is typical of this Liberal government that disregards the financial agreements made with the provinces in 1976, that makes changes in the established programs financing arrangements unilaterally, changes that will severely curtail health care and post-secondary education. It also eliminates revenue guarantees to provinces, as has been pointed out.
We also oppose the cutbacks, of course, which will create inequity and inequality in provincial health and education services. The cutbacks in this bill will allow and encourage the privatization of medicare, a process which has unfortunately already started in a number of provinces-the provinces particularly, 1 might mention, of Alberta and Ontario. It will make it difficult, more difficult indeed, for progressive governments, such as those of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, to
Federal Transfers to Provinces
continue universal health care for their citizens-a principle that 1 would hope all parties in this House would certainly endorse.
I want to concentrate on the community impact and the human impact on people in areas such as my riding of Vancouver East. They will suffer as health services are cut as a result of the cutbacks laid down in this bill. It is important that we not only maintain but extend our health care services with increased financing.
If we look at the demographic trends in the Canadian population, we see an aging population with many expensive health care needs. These will increase. It is important that these needs be met not by institutional and long-term care, but with preventive care so that our older population can remain in their homes as long as possible and receive support services in the community.
Those from the west know-and I must say the Liberal government is not tuned into this-that there is a new mobility pattern in our country. Thousands of people are moving west and north, particularly young people, in search of employment. There will be new communities in the future. Adequate health care services must be provided for workers in some of the more remote areas. Expensive new facilities such as hospitals will be required. Increasing unemployment and economic stress has created increased pressure for millions of people. This creates an impact on the need for physician and psychiatric care services. Increased poverty means poorer nutrition for children and young families, and as a result they will require increased health care, something they are entitled to in a country like Canada.
It is a federal responsibility to increase funding for medical research. For example, urea formaldehyde has been a frequent topic of discussion in this House. There are new environmental hazards as well as the impacts of microtechnology, particularly on women workers. All this is in addition to chronic illnesses such as cancer, heart disease and arthritis for which we have not yet found a cure. Therefore, there must be increased federal funding.
My colleague, the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) talked about the impact of these cutbacks on provinces such as Manitoba, so I will not dwell on this in my remarks. It is particularly important for the federal government to assist not only in maintaining but in improving health care services. I will not touch on post-secondary education; other colleagues will speak to this subject. It is a struggle just to maintain the status quo. In addition to investing funds, we must plan properly so that the health care dollar is better used. This may help to reduce or at least sustain the present level of health care costs.
Members opposite have said that the federal government made a mistake by moving into block funding for health care services. We agree it was a mistake. It gave up federal control over the need for general health care standards across this

March 24, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
country. It lost some of its negotiating power with the provinces with regard to insisting on certain priorities which are essential for a sound preventive health care program.
As I said, I want to concentrate on the human side of health care services and the kinds of services that will be affected by the federal cutbacks and, therefore, the lack of adequate funding to the provinces which are implied in this bill. It is also important to talk about the health needs of young children. I refer to reports presented to the House last spring by the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare and its recommendations with regard to young families, and the federal responsibility toward them.
Finally, in my remarks I will refer to concerns of the National Action Council on the Status of Women in its brief presented to the task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. It is concerned particularly with the health care of women in Canada.
First I want to talk about the type of health care services which will give us a more sensible and practical value for our dollar. This will help to alleviate some of the expenses of chronic institution care which consumes so much of the health care dollar. My party believes that not enough funding is given to medical care services, medical delivery systems and community health programs. I refer to programs that should be readily accessible to families and individuals in their neighbourhood, adapted to local conditions.
I wish to speak about the importance of community health clinics that are developed under the guidance of community boards which provide services geared to the ethnic make-up of many communities. My riding of Vancouver East is multiethnic. There is a large proportion of low-income people. The services they require must receive federal funding. They require demonstration grants from the federal government.
Some years ago in my riding a health centre was developed. It was established as a model for other clinics. It is called the Reach Clinic and was developed in co-operation with UBC medical services and local general practitioners. A community board runs the operation. It is a non-profit organization which employs workers from many different ethnic backgrounds. It serves a multi-ethnic community. There is a medical card which can be used by families for all health services. It was one of the first community clinics to develop a dental program for low-income families, a very important service that is not available in most communities.
Recently the Reach Clinic began a program for adolescent parents. I have talked before in the House about the extreme social and health problems caused by the great increase in adolescent pregnancies. There is a need for a whole range of support programs for teenage mothers. Many are really children trying to rear children of their own. This kind of clinic provides support for adolescent parents and education with regard to job training, and helps young mothers with child daycare programs so that they can get on with their lives knowing that their children are receiving proper care. It provides information on parenting skills, nutrition and an awareness of basic health needs.
The experience of health community clinics in Quebec adds another important dimension. I refer to the whole question of prevention. There are family-life education programs, access to contraceptives, and freedom of choice with regard to abortions which should be available through community health care clinics. In my riding we also have a downtown health society which was adapted to the needs of street people, including alcoholics, drug addicts and those who live in the downtown area of Vancouver. Most of these people have extremely low incomes, inadequate diets and severe health problems. Therefore this downtown clinic, again with a community board, stressed hot meals and good nutrition for street people. It helped to provide dental care to those who had no access to it and provided referrals to many community services.
In the Chinatown area next door, another health care concept is being developed as part of a social and co-operative housing project. This is largely for Chinese Canadian residents, many of whom are elderly and do not speak English. There are also many public housing projects in this community and, therefore, a public health department has agreed to decentralize and move into the basement of a new senior citizens development. This unit will be open to all residents of the community. It will provide a Cantonese-English-speaking staff as well as a community advisory committee. It is possible to adapt this centre to the needs and desires of elderly Chinese people to make available traditional herbal medicines and acupuncture in the future.
Another important health care centre is a day care centre for adults which provides medical care for the disabled and elderly. This will allow many of them to remain in their homes. Again, this centre would have a Cantonese staff, provide Cantonese meals, which will provide beneficial mental health and morale as well as good nutrition for these people.
I mention these examples because I believe it is extremely important that they be funded and not just maintained as demonstration projects. They should be expanded in every community, certainly throughout the metropolitan areas in Canada. This cannot be done without adequate funding and without fiscal arrangements which are fair to the provinces.
As I have mentioned, most of these services are provided in poverty areas. This requires a very high degree of subsidized care. For example, some centres in Victoria, Winnipeg and other cities have new health care clinics which have a combination of social services, health care services and a multiplicity of comprehensive support services. They provide services which prevent and cure the early symptoms of poor health which would ultimately relieve the expense of institutional care for these people.
As mentioned, there were a number of recommendations made by the subcommittee on the international year of the child to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs last spring. I would like to refer to a number of recommendations which were made on behalf of Canadian
March 24, 1982

children with regard to health services. There were several medical practitioners on the committee.
1 would like to refer to a few excerpts from this report, particularly from the section on children and health. It was felt by members of the committee that fetal and neonatal mortality and risk of handicaps are still substantial, varying widely from province to province. The recommendation went on to say:
The risk could be reduced with improved prenatal care. A key issue is the need for a system of reproductive care that provides among other things: regular care and supervision for all mothers during pregnancy: information for parents about the effects on the unborn of nutrition, smoking, and alcohol and drug usage during pregnancy; and good prenatal child care.
There was also considerable concern that with our sophisticated medical practices in Canada, many Canadian children are not being adequately immunized. It was recommended in particular that an extensive public education program be undertaken through federal and provincial co-operation to make the public more aware of the effects on the fetus of maternal nutrition, smoking and the use of drugs and alcohol during pregnancy and to stress the importance of immunization for young children.
You may think that this does not apply to the bill under discussion today but I can assure you that these recommendations relate very directly to the need for adequate funding for health care and preventive services to provide for the future good health of our children.
It was also proposed that family allowances should be extended so that mothers at the time of pregnancy will receive the proper nutrition to provide proper prenatal health care so that children will be born well developed physically and mentally.
The committee also stressed the quality of nutrition, which ties in very closely with health services and preventive health care, which is of serious concern, particularly the entire diet provided to children from low-income families.
I saw examples of inadequate diets for many children when I worked in co-operative food stores in public housing projects where children of families on very low-income used their money for junk food. This is not only true for low-income families but these families do not have the money for nutritious foods. Positive steps must be taken for adequate nutrition. Nutrition programs should be made available in preschool and elementary school hot lunch programs.
Another recommendation was to consider having more nonprofit food banks operating on a permanent basis in Canada for distribution to those in need.
I would indicate that this report has never been dealt with in the House. It has not gone to cabinet and has not been considered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). I consider this to be a disgrace after the amount of work that has been put into this report, not only by the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs but also by many voluntary groups across Canada.
Another problem severely affecting young people, predominately from the age group from 15 to 19 years, is suicide.
Federal Transfers to Provinces
Preventive measures must also be adopted to avoid fatal accidents. We also advocated recommendations based on studies which reveal the increasing number of adolescents who are using tobacco, alcohol and drugs, and we recommended that school help programs should stress the dangers of the use and abuse of such drugs. It was our belief that there should be a national advertising campaign warning against the harmful effects of drug abuse. Also, education and treatment service should be provided to control drug and alcohol abuse among the employed. This should not be a matter of concern only to the unions who are launching programs to improve the health conditions of workers, but to employers as well.
Those are some of the recommendations in the report on children and the need for federal funding to be continued and expanded for the preventive health care services.
In the alternate report which 1 presented to that committee on behalf of our party, I also stressed the importance of expanding the public health facility to enable health care nurses to reach out into the community, particularly homes where families are not likely to be using traditional medical services. Health care nurses should meet with young mothers to get them involved in supportive services and provide the kinds of health care services that are needed at a very early age so that children will have a better future.
Finally, if time permits, I would like to raise some of the points respecting health care cutbacks, which are of particular concern to women in Canada. These points were raised in a brief submitted to the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women in July, 1981. The National Action Committee stated:
-health care is an area of particular concern to women . . . Women arc much more frequently diagnosed as suffering from health problems than men are. Women feel the effects of federal and provincial cutbacks in health care more severely since they are the principal consumers of health care services.
Health care cutbacks put women in a double jeopardy position. First, the unequal treatment of women causes them to have higher rates of health breakdowns and second, society restricts their access to the means of ameliorating their health problems.
We are also concerned with the cutbacks in the funding of health care services from the standpoint of women as workers. Except for the highly skilled positions of doctors or managerial staff ... the majority of workers in the health care system-
By far, are women.
The fact that this committee invited both the Canadian Nurses Association and NAC's member group, the Canadian Union of Public Employees, to make representations at its hearings indicates that the committee recognizes the enormous implications of the cutbacks for the women who work in hospitals.
From the perspective of women, both as consumers of health care services and as workers in the health care system, we arc tremendously concerned by the overall decrease in funding as well as the elimination of mandatory federal-provincial cost-sharing formulae.
With the introduction of the Established Programs Financing (EPF) arrangements in 1977, the federal government limited its expenditure increases to the over-all growth in the economy and eliminated conditional grants in favour of cash and tax-point transfers to the provinces. While this change was supposed

March 24, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
to give the provinces greater autonomy in the health care field, it has simply meant that there has been a substantial decrease in health care funding on both the federal and the provincial levels. The provinces have used the introduction of the EPF system as a means of decreasing their share of health expenditures. In 1975-76, the provincial share of health care expenditures was 41 per cent of the total. In 1980-81, it dropped to 27.8 per cent of the total moneys expended. By allowing the provinces to evade their responsibility in this area, severely restricting its own contribution to health care, the federal government has reneged on its commitment to the Canadian people to provide equality of access and a quality health care service from coast to coast.
Quality health care is our right. It is not a privilege conferred upon us by our federal or provincial governments. The National Action Committee, therefore, demands that the over-all level of funding from both federal and provincial governments for health care services be increased substantially and that the federal government reinstitute a cost-sharing formula to ensure that the provincial governments live up to their responsibilities. It is clear to us that block funding is ineffective: the provinces are not sufficiently committed to the delivery of quality health care services without some form of incentive-
Cutbacks in post-secondary education have more or less followed the same pattern as the cutbacks in health care, with the result that there are fewer places open in post-secondary institutions, fewer jobs, and the cost of users is escalating.
This affects women particularly.
Women's access to post-secondary training has traditionally been severely limited because of discrimination in selection and lack of resources.
This lack refers to education training resources. I might add that there is a lack of adequate manpower allowances and a lack of daycare to go along with them. The brief goes on to read:
Eighty per cent of women in the paid labour force are concentrated in five low-paying employment ghettos: clerical/secretarial, small manufacturing, hospital work, teaching and services. These five areas are the very ones that will be most severely affected as a result of the introduction of micro-processing technologies over the next two to five years.
Paid employment is the fundamental right of every adult who wants it and if women are not, once again, to be pushed out of the labour force, massive job retraining in the non-traditional areas of employment as well as in new technical sectors must be provided to them. To cut back post-secondary education funding at a time when women are going to be facing a technologically-induced employment crisis is to effectively bar women from the labour force. The National Action Committee, on behalf of the more than three million women that it represents through its member groups, strenuously objects to any policy that negatively affects the employment prospects of women. We demand that our federal and provincial governments immediately expand funding for postsecondary institutions and make every effort to ensure that women are recruited for training and retraining, as well as for jobs in these institutions.
Recently, women in Canada have witnessed the severe contraction of subsidized child care spaces, rules to limit access further, the lowering of standards, and the introduction of child care businesses that cut corners and make profits at the expense of our children. The National Action Committee vehemently opposes any effort by our governments to transfer responsibility for child care from the public to the private sector. One of the original bases upon which NAC was founded was to fight for a publicly funded, twenty-four hour, free, child care system that would be accessible to all.
I can tell hon. members that this party soundly endorses that recommendation. The brief goes on to say:
The National Action Committee is concerned because recent cutbacks in day care funding and the refusal of our governments to regard child care as anything but a welfare service have restricted access to the already-inadequate child care system and resulted in the lowering of standards and in poor wages and working conditions for child care workers, almost all of whom are women. We would like to reiterate most strongly the demand, articulated by women across Canada, for a free, universally-accessible, twenty-four-hour child care system.
In this area, we are particularly concerned that an incentive funding program be developed to force provinces to provide adequate levels of funding and ensure that uniform, quality services are available from coast to coast. A cost-sharing approach will no doubt give the federal government the much needed incentive to
drastically expand child care, as well as provide provinces with the necessary stimulus to develop the programs.
We would like to point out here that if the federal government is genuinely committed to the principle of economic equality for women, a principle to which it has so often paid lip service-
But done little.
-it must initiate action on this fundamental underpinning of women's equality-a good child care system available and accessible to all. The federal government can no longer hide behind the argument that this is a matter for provincial jurisdiction. The time for child care has come.
A number of other issues could be raised on behalf of women, and I am sure other speakers will be raising them, but since my time is now up, I would just like to stress once again the importance of an adequate federal funding program for health care services and post-secondary services, particularly for women in Canada and their children, who must have a better start in life.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise to speak in criticism of Bill C-97. Although some of the points that I will make have been touched upon already, I shall make them again, as well as some more specific points, because they bear repetition and clarification.
As well as being arbitrary and one-sided in the way it has been handled in comparison with the tradition of federal-provincial negotiations, this bill also represents very interesting manoeuvring on the part of the federal government to make the principle of federal-provincial negotiations fairly unworkable. Delays were introduced which had the result of making it impossible to meet the timetable set for serious negotiations.
First of all, I want to comment on some of the effects of the cuts that have been envisaged and about which we have been warned and which, to some extent, have already occurred.
In the riding of Spadina and in the city and province in which it is located, cutbacks in education and health care services and specifically post-secondary education are already being experienced. The federal government will maintain that this is all the fault of the provincial government, yet it seems to give different figures at different times. For example, at the present time a figure in the range of 55 per cent of the funding for post-secondary education in Ontario is given by federal government spokesmen. I remember that last summer a spokesman for the federal government claimed that it was contributing 87 per cent of the cost of post-secondary education at places like the University of Toronto. That statement came from a person who had been engaged, as secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in a good deal of the planning and manupulation of the figures. He was hoping to move further up the ladder and into cabinet. I refer, of course, to Jim Coutts, the one and always aspirant to election in Spadina. He stood in front of the university, at Convocation Hall, and asserted that this government was paying 87 per cent of the cost of universities such as the University of Toronto. Since then other government spokesmen have said it is paying something like 50 or 55 per cent. Either the government has
March 24, 1982

cut its contribution by almost half within a few months or the figures given by one spokesman or another are not to be believed.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, the effect of cuts by both the federal government and the provincial government of Ontario are already being felt in the area of post-secondary education in the province. Next fall the fees will be raised by at least 12 per cent, and when the cuts now proposed by the federal government go into effect, the fees will undoubtedly be raised again for 1983. There have been cuts in programs at the University of Toronto, Queen's University and colleges such as St. Lawrence and St. Clair. There is a general cut in accessibility. During the past year 50,000 student applications were rejected by the post-secondary education system in Ontario because places were not available. In fact, only 45 per cent of applicants for 1980 and 1981 were accepted. There simply is not enough room to educate the students we have, even though the ratio of university educated people to population is lower in this country than it is in the United States and Japan.
What is happening is that the money envisaged as being withheld from post-secondary education as such, is to be recycled into specific job training tailored to particular job needs. That does not provide the equivalent of a genuine postsecondary education which the country needs and which many other countries still provide.
There is, in fact, no attempt to set any sort of minimum standard on post-secondary education. There is no standard of accessibility relating to the poor, the immigrant, the native peoples. There is no standard of quality in education. Of course, the trouble is that the government which enacted the original legislation for EPF and revenue guarantees failed to ensure any such guarantees. It claimed that if the matter went badly it would ensure them, but now it is backing out.
In the field of health, such a well-known hospital as Toronto Western has closed its obstetrics department. This was not done cheerfully, the director told me, but after great heartsearching. There were operating deficits and something had to go, so now the obstetrics department has gone from one of the major hospitals of our country. Previously, that hospital had closed wards and made other cost-cutting moves. Such things do not contribute to the wellbeing of any hospital. There have also been cuts in public health services in Toronto and other cities and municipalities.
Of course, the general cuts in hospitals have, through antiunion legislation, mainly been borne by the nurses, nursing aides, orderlies and cafeteria workers. While doctors are allowed to strike-just like the Tories-nurses are not allowed to strike, and hospital support workers are thrown in jail for doing what doctors and Tories do with impunity.
OHIP fees have been raised and hospitals are inventing all kinds of new fees for patients. Things that were previously part of the service are now not available under QHIP but are charged separately. Hospital admissions have slowed down, and there have been cases of serious illness or injury where people were not treated in time because of delays in admissions. There have also been cases where people have been discharged prematurely, evidently because of over crowding
Federal Transfers to Provinces
once certain wards and facilities were reduced. There have been cases where people were discharged prematurely and their health suffered afterwards, even to the point of death in some cases.
The point is that the government introduced Bill C-97 which, if it passes in its present form, would amend current legislation and result in changes to two of the most important programs developed in this country, the established programs financing and fiscal equalization.
We in the New Democratic Party are deeply concerned with the reduction in federal funding for essential social programs and by the government's refusal to work co-operatively with the provinces in order to ensure first-rate education, health and other basic public services.
I want to comment now on the established programs financing and how it evolved for health care and post-secondary education. Federal transfers to the provinces originated in the imbalance between federal and provincial expenditure responsibilities and revenue capacities. Under the BNA Act the responsibility for health, education and welfare resides with the provinces. After World War II the federal government used its superior fiscal resources to initiate a number of national shared cost programs in these areas. These major new programs were designed to ensure that national standards in the quality of health and education programs delivered by the provinces would be achieved. This undertaking that certain standards would be achieved and maintained was made at that time.
Throughout the late 1960s and the early 1970s the federal government became increasingly alarmed by the rapid growth in its financial transfers to the provinces for hospital insurance, medicare and post-secondary education. Over the strong objections of the provinces, many of which could never have participated in these national programs without substantial federal cost sharing, the federal government instituted a number of arbitrary and controversial measures to cut back its contributions to these programs.
Federal contributions to post-secondary education programs were capped in 1973-1974. In 1975 the federal government announced a schedule of annual ceilings to its medicare contributions, and gave its notice of intention to terminate the hospital insurance agreements in 1980.
Reacting in part to the unanimous concern expressed by the provinces over this arbitrary imposition of ceilings and in part to continuing concern about the rate of increase of its contributions, the federal government proposed new funding arrangements for health and post-secondary education in 1976. Effective April 1, 1977, federal conditional grants to the provinces in support of hospital insurance, medical care and post-secondary education were replaced by the established programs financing arrangements that we now have. EPF replaced federal conditional cost-sharing payments in these program areas by unconditional cash grants, together with the

March 24, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
transfer of tax room from the federal to the provincial governments. The per capita federal EPF transfer to the provinces escalates annually at the rate of increase in the gross national product. It is calculated independently of provincial program expenditures. One of the important points is that the federal government knowingly separated its granting from any cooperation by the provinces; it foresaw the possibility that that co-operation would fail. It undertook to restore a requirement of co-operation, and it has now reneged on that undertaking.
There were five principles to the established program financing. They were announced by the Prime Minister at the conference of first ministers in June, 1976. First, the federal government should continue to pay a substantial share of program costs. Second, federal government payments should be calculated independently of provincial program expenditures. Third, there should be greater equality in per capita terms in federal contributions to the provinces. Fourth, funding arrangements should be permanent. Fifth, there should be continuing federal participation in the development of policies of national significance in health and post-secondary education.
These principles announced the end of traditional costsharing in hospital insurance, medical care and post-secondary education. An unconditional block funding arrangement was implemented with no matching requirements by provincial governments. Two restraint objectives were intended. The first introduced an element of certainty for the federal government in its financial commitment to these programs. The second provided increased flexibility for provincial budget planning to allow greater scope for cost-saving measures.
The principle of predictability and certainty of federal transfers was to give provinces the opportunity to undertake proper expenditure forecasting, secure in the knowledge that federal contributions would not be capped or withdrawn.
By establishing the financing of these programs on a permanent basis, the federal government attempted to alleviate provincial uncertainty concerning future federal contributions. At the June, 1976, conference the Prime Minister stated exclusively the federal government's commitment to the principle of long-term certainty. He said:
The fourth principle (of EPF) is that the arrangements be established on a more or less permanent footing, to reduce the uncertainty that has attended in the past the questions of continued federal involvement and the dimension of federal financial contributions . . . (notice of termination) would not be given lightly, because the intention is to underline the relative permanence and stability of the new arrangements.
Not all the provinces were encouraged by the new funding proposal. There are serious liabilities in having an unconditional block fund approach to federal financing of provincial programs when national standards in the quality of these services are paramount. Notwithstanding concerns, the actual financial offer made by the federal government was judged unacceptable by all provinces. In brief, the provinces were asked to assume all the financial risk in large program areas that were experiencing substantial cost pressures. Moreover, provinces were assuming this risk at the same time the federal government was proposing to terminate the 1972 revenue guarantee program.
The revenue guarantee was to become a central aspect of both the 1976 and 1981 negotiations on established programs financing. The revenue guarantee was introduced by the federal government in 1972 to encourage provinces to parallel federal income tax reform. It was a promise by the federal government that over a five-year period the provinces would lose no revenues by adopting the federal income tax changes. Although the provinces warned the federal government that the tax reform measures would significantly reduce revenues, the federal government insisted that the loss of revenue would be minimal. Ottawa optimistically assumed that revenue guarantee payments to the provinces would be small. Despite an arbitrary formula change by the federal government which reduced revenue guarantee payments to the provinces for 1974 and subsequent years, payments were nearly $1 billion per year by 1976 and were escalating.
Provincial estimates of the cost of tax reform have been absolutely correct. Termination of the revenue guarantee would severely disrupt provincial finances. Although the federal government recognized there would be a difficult period of adjustment for all provinces when the guarantee ended, it resolutely maintained that the guarantee would expire at the end of 1976.
Given the importance to provincial finances, the ten provincial premiers unanimously requested the transfer of four personal income tax points and associated equalization as partial compensation for the termination of this program. The stage was set for a major compromise.
Central to the negotiations was the federal government's legal commitment to cost-sharing under its hospital insurance agreements with the provinces until mid-1980. Provinces would have been entitled to claim any difference between this open-ended cost-sharing arrangement and the hospital insurance component of EPF for the first three years of the new program. The federal government wanted to get out of this commitment.
The federal government offered the provinces financial compensation. There was one equalized point of personal income tax plus an equivalent amount of cash for termination of the revenue guarantee. Significantly, the compensation for termination was included as a permanent part of the basic structure of the EPF arrangements and as an inseparable component of the contributions paid to the provinces for health and education. In exchange, the provinces agreed to waive their rights to open-ended cost-sharing under the hospital insurance agreements.
In the period 1977 to 1981 there were further major developments. Given federal assurances in 1976 that EPF was a permanent arrangement for funding of health care and higher education, the provinces had reasonable expectations that EPF would evolve smoothly. However, five major developments occurred over the last four years which put in question the federal government's real commitment to EPF, that is to
March 24, 1982

say, to the national health program and the post-secondary education system.
The first was the 1978 federal budget cuts. In August, 1978, the federal government announced significant budget cuts and a re-allocation of funds from existing programs to new priorities. Included were major unilateral cutbacks in federal-provincial transfers. At a November, 1978, finance ministers' meeting the federal finance minister suggested EPF would be the target for reductions. That proposal startled the provinces. EPF was not yet a year and a half old and was supposedly based on stability and predictability. In retrospect, this was the first indication that the federal government was anxious to back out of its financial commitment under EPF. The provinces, aware that reductions in federal funding would have lowered health and post-secondary education standards, rejected the federal proposals. As a result, the federal government cut back other transfer payments to the provinces.
Second was the federal allegations regarding the provincial misuse of EPF funds. Beginning in 1979 the federal government initiated an attack against the provinces, alleging provincial misuse of EPF funds. Provincial governments were accused of diverting medicare funds to other programs. These allegations precipitated a royal commission report on Canadian health services. Although the Hall commission report concluded that the provinces were not diverting health dollars, the federal campaign escalated up to and through the recent fiscal arrangements review. Over the past year provincial postsecondary education expenditures have become the favourite federal target. That there was an increase in federal contributions to the financing of health and post-secondary education in relation to provincial expenditures may be true, in some provinces, for the initial years of the new arrangements. This is not surprising, however, given the nature of the block-funding proposal introduced by the federal government.
One other technical feature of the EPF formula influenced the relative size of federal contributions in the initial years. Transfers to the provinces are escalated each year on the basis of a lagged three-year moving average of the growth in the national economy. During the early years of block funding the escalator was, to a considerable extent, based on the inflated but declining growth rate of the Canadian economy during the mid-1970s. This naturally inflated federal contributions to the established programs during the initial years. This was known to all governments in 1976 and its effects were predictable. The fact that EPF was deliberately front-end loaded during its introductory years, made this aspect of the formula an effective characteristic for selling the new arrangements to the provinces. It was also well understood in 1976 that provincial program costs would rise faster than federal contributions during a period of accelerating inflation. That is the current situation. In recent years provincial governments have been carrying an increasing portion of the accelerating health and education costs.
When the block funding arrangement was proposed in 1976, stable and predictable transfers for health and post-secondary education programs were primary objectives. These have been achieved by the current arrangements. Federal projections of
Federal Transfers to Provinces
the transfers under the EPF arrangements provided to the provinces in 1976 were extremely accurate; within 2 per cent of the amount actually transferred.
The third thing that happened in those four years, Mr. Speaker, was that the federal government became increasingly preoccupied with the lack of public visibility for federal transfers to the provinces. Given the nature of the block funding financing arrangements, it is no surprise that the federal government is having visibility problems with the EPF. As far as public accountability is concerned, the federal government not only can but is obliged to enforce the conditions specified in the national medical care and hospital insurance acts. If accountability is a problem, then the federal government is either not carrying out its obligations, or the specified conditions do not clearly spell out the respective responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments. It is a federal problem, not a provincial problem, and the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) and the Minister for National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) should get moving in carrying out their duty to enforce these principles of accountability and equal access to a quality level of care.
The fourth thing that happened in these years was the October, 1980, federal budget. The federal government indicated that it intended to achieve significant savings in social transfer payments to the provinces beginning in 198283. At the December 17, 1980, federal-provincial finance ministers' meeting the provinces urged the federal government to proceed with negotiations at the earliest possible date so that a mutually acceptable agreement could be reached in the interest of all Canadians. However, the federal finance minister was not willing to discuss the federal government's proposals at that time. He finally agreed to hold a meeting in March, 1981 but the meeting was never called.
At the western premiers' conference in Thompson, Manitoba, on April 28, 1981, and again at the meeting of the western provincial finance ministers and treasurers on May 5, 1981 in Victoria, the western provinces repeated their call to the federal government to table EPF proposals as soon as possible. Ottawa disregarded both requests. At the 22nd annual premiers' conference in August, 1981, the premiers were unanimous in agreeing that intergovernmental negotiations on EPF must commence immediately. Ottawa again ignored the provinces.
For more than an entire year, Mr. Speaker, Ottawa stonewalled the provinces in their repeated requests for ministerial negotiations on financial arrangements. The federal finance minister delayed meeting with his provincial counterparts until November 23, 1981, in Halifax. We must conclude that the federal timetable was designed to ensure there would be no time or opportunity for real negotiations and consultations.
The fifth thing to happen was the establishment of the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements in February, 1981. Its mandate was to examine fiscal arrangements within the context of the federal government's expenditure plan as set out in the October 28, 1980, budget. It

March 24, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
was to report to Parliament by the end of June, 1981. The main thrust of the federal finance minister's presentation to the task force was that transfers would have to be cut significantly to meet the federal government's over-all strategy of reducing its deficit. He implied that transfers were a major contributing factor to the federal deficit, and confirmed that the federal government was seeking net savings in social program transfers of $1.5 billion. In August, 1981, the task force released its report and flatly rejected that part of its terms of reference, requiring its examination to take place within the context of the October 28, 1980, federal budget.
In addressing the federal government's concerns about its deficit, the task force stated:
-federal grants to provinces and municipalities expressed as a percentage of total federal spending have been fairly constant since 1970. There is, therefore, no ground to suggest that the federal transfers have been getting out of hand. In fact, they grew at a slower rate in the 1970s than they did in the 1960s.
The task force rejected the arguments that federal-provincial transfers were responsible for the federal deficit. In the view of the task force, the federal deficit is the result of the general economic situation and federal tax and expenditure decisions. If the federal government gives away billions to the wealthiest corporations in this country and refuses to collect taxes from them, it is no wonder that the federal government has a deficit.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
In his presentation to the parliamentary task force, the chairman of the Economic Council of Canada likewise took issue with the federal finance minister's statements that transfers to the provinces must be cut to reduce the federal deficit. He said that one should seriously doubt the wisdom and fairness of solving the federal deficit problem by merely transferring the problem to the provinces. This is not a solution at all. In the summary and conclusions to its report, entitled "Financing Confederation Today and Tomorrow'', the Economic Council reiterated its position. The Council's first recommendation was that the federal government reconsider its proposed reduction in transfers to the provinces.
I now wish to look at the federal cutbacks to the EPF. The federal government announced in its November, 1981, budget that the changes to the established program financing arrangements were as follows: first, effective April 1, 1982, compensation to the provinces for the termination of the revenue guarantee which had been built into the EPF will be eliminated; second, as of April 1, 1982, federal contributions for health and post-secondary education programs will be on an equal per capita basis; and third, by March 31, 1983, new federal-provincial arrangements for the financing of post-secondary education and human resource development will be devised. If the provinces are unco-operative in developing these new arrangements the federal government will freeze future transfers to the provinces for post-secondary education at their 1982-83 levels. Fourth, by March 31, 1983, the national standards for health care are to be clarified and an effective mechanism for their maintenance is to be developed. This is to
be done in consultation with the provinces and incorporated in new federal health legislation.
The financial implications of these steps are as follows: the elimination of the revenue guarantee will save Ottawa $813.7 million in 1982-83 and $5,306.2 million over the five-year period of the 1982-87 fiscal arrangements. Savings to the federal government, by placing the EPF transfers on an equal per capita basis, will amount to $127.9 million in 1982-83 and $574.6 million over the next five-year period. In total, the federal government will cut back transfers for health and postsecondary education by $941.6 million in 1982-83 and by $5,880.8 million over the period 1982-83 to 1986-87. These cutbacks are substantially greater than the savings proposed in the federal budget of October, 1980.
What we have to consider is the misleading federal presentation and data errors. In its November, 1981, budget, the federal government attempted to mask the real impact of the cuts to the EPF by presenting tables which suggested that increased provincial revenues resulting from the tax increases contained in the federal budget would offset EPF cutbacks. This is extremely misleading. Any additional tax revenue received by the provinces is from provincial home source revenue. It is collected from provincial taxpayers as a provincial income tax. It is not a federal transfer. Moreover, in those years when the federal government instituted tax changes which reduced provincial home source revenues, there was no thought of compensating the provinces with increased federal transfers. Even if this tactic were acceptable, which it is not, the actual cost of the EPF cutbacks to the provinces was further misrepresented by massive errors in the federal budget. By its own admission, the federal government overestimated the alleged revenue increases to the provinces by almost $650 million.
The federal government has never presented the provinces with a complete EPF proposal. It has always split its negotiations and threats. The deadline of March 31, 1982, was set by the federal government for legislation on the financial aspects of the EPF. This was after the federal government delayed for a year the request of the provinces for negotiation on this very point. The deadline for legislation on program issues is March 31, 1983. The latter is accompanied by the threat to freeze federal payments for higher education if the provinces cannot agree to as yet unspecified federal conditions. The package is incomplete. It provides for financial cutbacks without first addressing the programs to be financed. This is a complete reversal of the proper process of review and negotiation. Definitive federal proposals with respect to health and higher education objectives and conditions have not yet been made. The federal initiatives are completely contrary to the principles outlined by the Prime Minister when he introduced EPF in 1976. Of course, if the Prime Minister resigns in the next month or two, he can slough off all responsibility for all of his promises.
In essence, the federal government is attempting to reduce its financial involvement while increasing its control over provincial spending in health and higher education.
March 24, 1982

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It should be noted that, except for a three-year notice of termination clause in the EPF arrangements, there is no legislative deadline for changes to EPF. Without legislative action, the existing financial arrangements will continue indefinitely, in keeping with the intended long-term nature of EPF. The federal government's stated intention to establish new financing arrangements for post-secondary education clearly indicates that it wishes to terminate the current EPF arrangements within one or two years. However, no notice of termination has been given in the House of Commons in spite of the Prime Minister's stated principle of permanency and stability. It is not known whether or not these new financing arrangements for post-secondary education will be accompanied by further cutbacks in federal funding for universities
Federal Transfers to Provinces
and technical schools. The pattern is clear, however. The federal government is seeking more political visibility for lower levels of spending without any concern for quality of services provided to Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, this bill is a bad one. I believe it should be voted down by this House. I hope that the federal government will seriously reconsider it and, particularly within the committee, will be willing to accept amendments.
